1.pericope_label: Israel pitches in the plains of Moab by Jordan near Jericho, and Balak the son of Zippor sees all that Israel had done to the Amorites

schools.summary: Calvin reads the alarm as proof that the reprobate are agitated by groundless terrors, the just reward of men who never sought peace with God, and frames the narrative as Satan turning from force of arms to snares while God makes his truth receive the testimony of its own enemies; Gill traces the route from Bashan and supplies the rabbinic reasoning attributed to Balak.

Henry shows the fear was needless, since Israel had been forbidden to contend with Moab, and draws the rule that those who design mischief pretend mischief is designed against them, their groundless jealousies colouring their causeless malice.

Clarke insists Israel had taken no land then belonging to Moab, only what Sihon had already taken from them, and places the camp on the east side over against Jericho; Wesley notes the plains kept their old name through two changes of owner.

Ellicott fixes the extent of the Arboth Moab and refuses to let the phrase “on this side Jordan” settle which bank is meant, the same Hebrew form being rendered both ways in the Authorised Version; Keil and Delitzsch step back to the halt’s purpose, a trial bearing on Israel’s relation to the heathen world and the close of Moses’ legislative work before his death.

debates: Which bank “on this side Jordan” denotes. Clarke and Wesley take it plainly as the east side over against Jericho; Ellicott holds that the Hebrew word cannot determine it, citing a chapter where the Authorised Version renders the same form both ways in consecutive clauses.

3.pericope_label: Moab is sore afraid because the people are many, and says to the elders of Midian, Now shall this company lick up all that are round about us, as the ox licketh up the grass of the field

schools.summary: Gill measures the panic across king, nobles and people, reads it as fulfilling a prophecy of Moses, reports two rabbinic accounts of the relation between Moab and Midian without choosing between them, and distinguishes this northern Midian near the Arnon from the Midian of Jethro.

Ellicott denies any ground for the fear, since Israel had been forbidden to contend with Moab, while allowing that Balak may not have known it and that an earlier refusal of passage explains the alarm; he suggests Balak may himself have been a Midianite imposed as king by the Amorites, and finds the ox at grass a comparison suited to a pastoral people; Keil and Delitzsch turn to the site of Pethor and judge the attempted identifications uncertain.

Wesley traces the fright to the promise that the dread of Israel should fall on all nations and to the particular word about Moab, gathers the titles the Midianite elders carry elsewhere, and glosses the verb as consuming utterly, the sense in which fire licks up water and sacrifices.

debates: What Moab and Midian were to each other. Gill sets one rabbinic account, which makes them a single people or long-standing allies, against another, which makes them enemies who patched up a peace only for fear of Israel; Wesley treats them as separate kingdoms united by a common enemy.

5.pericope_label: He sent messengers unto Balaam the son of Beor to Pethor, saying, Behold, there is a people come out from Egypt which cover the face of the earth, and they abide over against me

schools.summary: Gill rejects each rabbinic identification of Balaam in turn and denies he was ever a good man or true prophet, Scripture calling him a diviner; Calvin finds the case instructive because it begins well, Balak’s distrust of human aid deserving praise while his route to God does not, since he devises his own means, purchases incantations from a mercenary prophet and is satisfied with a venal blessing where he should have asked what God willed.

Wesley holds that Balaam is called a prophet because God inspired him to speak what follows, and reports the Jewish view that he had once been a great prophet from whom God departed for his covetousness; he takes the two forms of the father’s name as simply two names, and places Pethor in Mesopotamia by the Euphrates; Clarke reports the objection that the description fits any river anywhere and adopts the Samaritan reading “Ammon” for “his people”, supported by a dozen Hebrew manuscripts and two versions.

Ellicott derives both names from roots meaning to devour and to consume, taken to mark a family in which magic was hereditary, explains the New Testament variant by a pronunciation of the guttural, keeps the received text and construes it rather than emending, and identifies the river as the Euphrates; Keil and Delitzsch confess the town unknown.

debates: What Balaam was. Gill denies he was ever a true prophet, since Scripture names him a diviner; Wesley grants him a genuine prophetic gift, lost afterwards through covetousness; Ellicott treats the very names as marking a hereditary family trade in magic.

Where Pethor stood and how the clause should read. Clarke adopts an emendation reading “Ammon” for “his people”, on the ground that the received text fits any river in any country; Ellicott keeps the text and construes it differently, placing Pethor in Mesopotamia on the Euphrates, where Wesley also places it, while Keil and Delitzsch judge the site unknown.

6.pericope_label: Balak asks Balaam to curse this people, for he whom thou blessest is blessed; and the elders of Moab and Midian depart with the rewards of divination in their hand

schools.summary: Gill takes the elders for princes and nobles and infers from the presence of both nations that they made common cause whatever their political relation.

Clarke holds that Balaam was once a prophet of the true God who added sorcery to a poetic gift, supplies the belief that a curse could confound designs and drain strength, transcribes two ancient Roman forms for calling a city’s tutelary gods away and devoting it to ruin, and takes the gifts to include the costly materials of the incantation as well as a fee; Wesley paraphrases the request and catches the division of labour, imprecations on one side and the sword on the other.

Ellicott notes that Balak believed in the efficacy of the incantations, that Scripture celebrates the turning of the curse into a blessing as a favour to Israel, and that the phrase is literally “the divinations”, which he takes for the rewards rather than the instruments on the analogy of the word for glad tidings; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion from a second parallel and record that Balaam lodged the deputation overnight to learn what the Lord would say.

debates: What the “rewards of divination” were. Ellicott reports a reading that makes them instruments of divination and prefers the sense of wages, arguing from a parallel word; Keil and Delitzsch argue the same from two parallels; Clarke wants both, taking the gift to have covered the expensive materials of the rite as well as the soothsayer’s fee.
Whether Balaam had ever been a true prophet. Clarke states plainly that he once was one of the true God, against the flat denial recorded earlier in the chapter.
outliers: Clarke leaves the verse to transcribe at length two Latin incantation formulae used against Carthage.

8.pericope_label: And he said unto them, Lodge here this night, and I will bring you word again, as the Lord shall speak unto me: and the princes of Moab abode with Balaam

schools.summary: Gill reads the invitation as showing an immediate inclination to take the work, guesses at the nightly methods by which Balaam got his knowledge, and allows it may equally have been a way of gaining time; Calvin argues that a man waiting on the true God was probably no mere sorcerer and did hold the gift of prophecy, then distinguishes that gift from the office of the true prophets, who spoke only out of God’s mouth, were the organs of the Spirit for every necessary prediction, interpreted the Law and ratified the covenant, whereas Balaam had a particular gift only, was right in some things and wrong in others, and uttered bare revelations without doctrine, God willing such men among the heathen so that the excuse of ignorance should be taken away.

Clarke takes the verse to show that Balaam knew the true God and was used to consulting him; Wesley notes the night as God’s usual time for revelation by dreams, and offers two motives for naming Jehovah, reputation or the design of engaging Israel’s own God against them, as besiegers called out the god of a city.

Ellicott finds the true character of Balaam in the delay, since a prophet of the Lord must have known that cursing Israel was sin, and notes that the name of Jehovah was plainly known to him; Keil and Delitzsch record the express prohibition and the embassy sent back empty.

debates: What kind of prophet Balaam was. Clarke and Wesley credit him with genuine dealings with the true God; Gill had denied it outright; Calvin mediates by granting him the gift of prophecy while denying him the office, since he lacked the perpetual commission, the teaching function and the constancy that marked the true prophets.
Why Balaam names the Lord. Wesley offers reputation or strategy, and prefers the strategy, that Israel could only be ruined by turning their own God against them.

9.pericope_label: God comes to Balaam and asks, What men are these with thee? and Balaam repeats to him the message Balak had sent

schools.summary: Gill supposes the visitation came in a dream, as to Abimelech and Laban, and credits Balaam with reporting Balak’s message exactly, since he knew he could not deceive an omniscient God however easily he might conceal the truth from men.

Ellicott sets the question beside those put to Elijah at Horeb and to Hezekiah after the Babylonian embassy, all calculated to rouse a slumbering conscience, and would render the report “the people which came out from Egypt, it covereth” rather than the indefinite English.

Wesley takes the question as asked so that Balaam, repeating the business in God’s presence, might be ashamed of the folly of offering his services in it, and so that a foundation might be laid for the answer to follow.

12.pericope_label: God forbids Balaam to go or to curse the people, for they are blessed; he sends the princes away, and they report to Balak that Balaam refuses to come

schools.summary: Gill reads the words as refusing Balak’s first request and notes the promptness on both sides; Calvin builds the prophetic office on the reason given, prophets being only heralds of a grace God bestows at his own pleasure, so that blessing without commission is blasphemous, and then denies that Balaam’s obedience came from the heart, since a sincere man would have said it was useless to send at all, whereas a faltering excuse inflamed the king and raised the price.

Clarke restricts the prohibition to going in order to curse, since Balaam afterwards went by God’s own direction, and defends him against a charge he reports, that the message was whittled down from hand to hand until only a human refusal reached Balak; Balaam, he answers, could not have been more explicit than he was.

Ellicott observes that Balaam did not tell the messengers the ground of the prohibition, so that Balak could hope stronger inducements would prevail; Keil and Delitzsch read the king’s response as taking the refusal either for a weakly fear of God or for a ruse to get better terms, since a heathen who saw only a national god thought gods as well as men could be bought with honours.

debates: How honest Balaam’s refusal was. Clarke reports and rejects the charge that he suppressed part of God’s answer, holding that he spoke as positively as he could; Ellicott finds a real omission, the ground “for they are blessed”; Calvin goes furthest, reading the refusal as outwardly correct and inwardly false, framed to invite a better offer.

15.pericope_label: Balak sends princes more and more honourable, promising to promote Balaam to very great honour and to do whatsoever he says, if only he will come and curse this people

schools.summary: Gill supposes Balak thought the first deputation had slighted him, weighs whether the promise was office or wealth and allows both, and notes that great men did not think the errand beneath them; Calvin reads the embassy as the pride of superstition, which parades dignity as though grandeur could dazzle God, and then withdraws the credit he first gives Balaam’s reply, since a man who asks leave to enquire again is deliberating whether what God once prescribed must stand, and in effect asking God to deny himself.

Henry lays out the temptation in three parts — grander messengers, an urgent request that nothing hinder him, and terms left blank — and turns the king’s persistence into a reproach, since sinners stoop to any pains for their malice while we are close-handed in complying with virtue.
Keil and Delitzsch take the reply at face value, an inability flowing from moral awe of God and dread of his punishment, firmly established in Balaam’s mind from beginning to end.

debates: How to read Balaam’s magnificent refusal. Keil and Delitzsch take it as genuine, grounded in awe of God; Calvin grants the words their nobility and denies the speaker any, holding that a man who keeps the traffickers by him and asks again for a ruling he already has is boasting rather than obeying.

What Balak actually promised. Gill sets a reading of the doubled Hebrew phrase as immense wealth against the plain sense of court preferment, and allows both, noting that Balaam’s own answer speaks of silver and gold.

18.pericope_label: Balaam answers that if Balak gave him his house full of silver and gold he could not go beyond the word of the Lord his God, and asks the messengers to tarry another night that he may know what the Lord will say more

schools.summary: Gill reads the request to tarry as self-condemning, since a man who meant what he had just said would have sent the embassy home at once instead of giving it hope, and notes that the men addressed were officers of state as well as princes.

Clarke gives the answer full credit, since Balaam knew God too well to think his purposes reversible and respected him too much to act without leave, and defends the second enquiry as an innocent hope of further light; he also quotes the reproach that many make Balaam’s professions and would not do for a house full of gold what they do for a handful.

Ellicott offers the answer as either an ostentatious show of disinterestedness or a genuine consciousness of not speaking from himself, and condemns the second enquiry outright, since Balaam knew God does not repent and yet hoped to be allowed to curse the blessed; Keil and Delitzsch carry the narrative forward to the kindling of God’s anger and the angel standing in the way.

debates: Whether asking a second time was innocent. Clarke defends it as seeking further light that God might well have given; Gill holds that the request itself betrays the inclination, since an honest refusal would have sent the messengers home; Ellicott calls it a vain expectation entertained against what Balaam knew of God’s constancy.

20.pericope_label: God comes to Balaam at night and tells him that if the men come to call him he may rise and go, but shall speak only the word God gives him; and Balaam rises, saddles his ass and goes with the princes of Moab

schools.summary: Calvin holds that Balaam wanted God to belie himself, so that God ironically permits what he had forbidden, loosing the reins to a man obstinate in his own perverseness as one might emancipate an ungovernable son, and warns that reopening what God has decided is an attempt to bend him by importunity; Gill observes that Balaam rose early and did not wait to be called, which showed how intent he was on the journey.

Wesley states the condition plainly; Clarke reports a grammatical argument that it was never met, the Hebrew pronoun marking a man who acts out of his own head, so that Balaam went uncalled and there his iniquity chiefly lay, and closes with the reflection that many are restrained from sin merely by fear.

Ellicott denies any inconsistency with the earlier prohibition, which bore on the cursing, and reads the permission as a judgment, God letting transgressors eat the fruit of their own way; he also renders the condition as “forasmuch as the men have come to call thee”, since they had already come for that purpose.

debates: Whether the condition attached to the permission was fulfilled. Clarke reports and adopts a reading in which the pronoun marks Balaam going of his own head, uncalled, so that the fault lies precisely there, and Gill agrees from the narrative that he did not wait; Ellicott construes the clause as stating that the men had already come to call him, which removes the test altogether.

How the permission squares with the prohibition. Ellicott distinguishes the cursing, absolutely forbidden, from the journey, forbidden in mercy and then enjoined in judgment; Calvin makes the permission ironical, a loosing of the reins rather than a change of mind.

22.pericope_label: God’s anger is kindled because he went, and the angel of the Lord stands in the way for an adversary against him; he was riding upon his ass, and his two servants were with him

schools.summary: Calvin asks how God can be angry at what he permitted and answers that he permits much he does not approve, instancing flesh in the wilderness and the writing of divorce, so that Balaam deserved death for pertinaciously urging what was sinful; he meets the objection that the sentence is ill-proportioned beside the prophet struck down for eating bread, holding that Balaam’s punishment was delayed rather than remitted, and fastens on the disgrace of a glory revealed first to the ass; Gill assembles four grounds for the anger, the unmet condition, the suppressed prohibition, the settled will to curse, and a leave given in anger.

Henry holds that sin is not less provoking because permitted, since God suffers sin and is angry at it still, and that nothing displeases him more than designs against his people; he reads the angel as the promised enmity against Israel’s enemies, takes the holy angels for adversaries of sin employed more than we know, and observes that this one was Balaam’s adversary only because Balaam counted him so.

Ellicott finds the fault in the tense, a participle marking a continuous act, so that Balaam deliberately and resolutely went on in defiance of the warnings, and would render the angel as stationing himself in the way.

Wesley makes the unmet condition the whole fault, since Balaam rose and called the princes instead of waiting to be called, and cites the apostle’s verdict that he ran greedily into an error for reward; he takes the angel to have come to oppose if not to kill, and explains the small escort by the simplicity of those times.

debates: Why God was angry at a journey he had allowed. Calvin distinguishes what God permits from what he approves and locates the sin in the pertinacious urging; Henry states the same principle as a rule about permitted sin and adds the malice against God’s people; Gill lists four grounds together; Wesley and Ellicott both find it in the manner of setting out, the one in an unmet condition and the other in a tense of settled resolve.

23.pericope_label: The ass sees the angel with drawn sword and turns aside, is crushed against the vineyard wall, and at last falls down under Balaam, who smites her three times

schools.summary: Gill holds that Balaam’s eyes were held by God so that he might be rebuked by his own beast, which had sight he was denied, leaving him little reason to boast of open eyes; he reads the drawn sword as signifying the death Balaam would actually die, and explains the three sightings by an angel who disappeared between stations and stood visible again at each.

Clarke generalises the beast’s sight into the rule that a vision is given to those concerned while others in the same company see nothing, and quotes a reading of the angel’s three positions as the stages of God’s judgments, a rod shaken, an easy correction, and at last a strait with no turning.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the walled pass among the vineyards and the narrower place beyond it, where the animal could neither turn nor pass and so lay down; Ellicott would render the second station the hollow pass of the vineyards and the barriers fences rather than walls.

28.pericope_label: And the Lord opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?

schools.summary: Gill rejects both the charge of incredibility and the Jewish expedient of making the episode visionary, and argues that the heathen can hardly object given their own reports of a speaking ass, a speaking horse and a speaking ox; Calvin meets the sceptics on principle, asking whence men have speech at all and how parrots imitate a voice, denies that God is bound by the order he once appointed, and holds that the words were drawn from the beast without intelligence or judgment, adding that a direct rebuke by the angel would have lacked the ignominy the case required.

Clarke relocates the wonder, since an ass could open her own mouth only by a marvel while God opening it is no marvel at all, notes that Balaam shows no surprise because he saw whose doing it was, and pointedly declines to rehearse the heathen stories of speaking animals; Wesley says the power of speech and reasoning was conferred on her for that time.

Ellicott answers the subjective reading with two arguments: that consistency would make the angel subjective too, and then subjective to the ass, which crosses the line between intelligent and brute creation further than speech does; and that the narrative gives no hint of mixed interpretation while the apostle’s words could hardly be more suggestive of a literal fact.

debates: What the ass received. Wesley says speech and reasoning together for that occasion; Calvin expressly denies the second, holding that the words came without intelligence or judgment.

Whether the episode was outward or subjective. Ellicott states and refutes the subjective reading; Gill rejects an older version of it, the Jewish view that the whole was done in vision and never literally performed.
outliers: Gill supports the possibility from pagan fables of talking animals, precisely the material Clarke refuses to reproduce.

29.pericope_label: Balaam answers the ass that she has mocked him and that he would kill her had he a sword; and the ass asks whether she was ever wont to do so unto him

schools.summary: Gill prefers “defiled me” to “mocked me”, since she had run him against a wall and lain down with him in the dust, doubts the sense of mocking where only servants were present, and offers “sought occasion” as an alternative; he marvels that the beast replied as one who understood, and so had reasoning as well as speech.

Keil and Delitzsch render the charge that she had played him ill, and read the second speech as a plea from long service whose truth Balaam had to admit, which roused him from his blindness so that God could open his eyes; Ellicott renders the phrase literally “ever since thou livedst”, supports so long a service from an Arabic report quoted out of Gill, and turns the formula “unto this day” to show that it need not imply a long interval.

Wesley explains the absence of terror at a speaking beast either by a man used to conversing with evil spirits in such shapes or by one so blinded with passion that he never considered the strangeness of it.

debates: What the verb rendered “mocked” means. Gill argues for defiled or rolled in the dirt, or else for seeking occasion, on the ground that mockery makes little sense before servants only; Keil and Delitzsch render it played me ill.
outliers: Ellicott leaves the verse to draw a general conclusion about the formula “unto this day” elsewhere in the Pentateuch.

31.pericope_label: The Lord opens Balaam’s eyes and he sees the angel with drawn sword, and bows his head and falls flat on his face; and the angel asks why he has smitten his ass, for his way is perverse

schools.summary: Gill prefers held eyes to blindness, since Balaam could see his ass but not the angel, as Elisha’s servant could see the host but not the fiery chariots; Calvin makes perception a gift God sustains or extinguishes at pleasure, reads the prostration as the fear of a hypocrite that lasts only while the presence weighs on him, and exposes the offer to turn back “if it displease thee” as a pretence of doubt about what was already clear.
Ellicott would render the charge not that the way is perverse but that it leads to destruction in the angel’s sight.
Wesley takes the prostration as reverence and submission, and traces the perverseness of the way to covetousness.

debates: What the angel’s charge means. The English makes it a verdict on the character of the way; Ellicott renders it a statement about where the way leads; Wesley keeps the moral sense and identifies covetousness as its root.

33.pericope_label: And the ass saw me and turned from me these three times: unless she had turned from me, surely now also I had slain thee, and saved her alive

schools.summary: Gill states the case plainly: the ass saw what Balaam did not, that was why she turned, it was well for him that she did, and he should not have struck her.

Wesley reads the words as saying that Balaam alone would have been killed and the ass spared, so that her turning was wholly for his benefit and his anger against her unjust; Clarke widens it into a reflection on how often the meanest animals and most trivial occurrences preserve our lives and save our souls.

Keil and Delitzsch reject the traditional rendering as indefensible by the rules of the language and read a broken-off sentence in which the angel merely hints that the animal turned from affection to her master and was beaten for that very service; Ellicott adopts the same reading and cites the other commentator by name.

debates: How the verse should be construed. Keil and Delitzsch hold the traditional conditional rendering ungrammatical and substitute a broken sentence the hearer must complete, and Ellicott follows them; Clarke and Wesley keep the traditional sense and draw the moral from it.

34.pericope_label: Balaam says he has sinned, since he knew not that the angel stood in the way, and offers to turn back if it displease him; the angel bids him go with the men but speak only the word given him

schools.summary: Gill limits the confession to the beating of the ass and denies any sense of the covetousness or the intention behind the journey, and calls the permission a bare concession that gives a man up to his own lusts; Calvin makes the permission ironical, distinguishes what God does not approve from what he nevertheless chooses shall be done, illustrates from Jeroboam and Jehu, both used and both guilty, and holds that God meant to prove by Balaam’s own mouth how unchangeable his adoption of the people was.

Clarke takes the confession as proof that Balaam still feared God, since he offers to abandon the enterprise, and reproaches readers whose piety does not reach so far; Wesley states the permission as terms allowed.

Ellicott reads the repeated command as a punishment by which the prophet is made to reap the fruit of his own perversity, and notices that the angel identifies himself with the one who sent him, saying that the word he speaks is what Balaam must speak; Keil and Delitzsch record the departure with the princes.

debates: How much the confession covers. Gill confines it to the beating of the ass and denies any repentance of the covetousness behind the journey; Clarke takes the same words as evidence of a real fear of God, since Balaam offers to abandon the errand altogether.

36.pericope_label: Balak goes out to meet Balaam at a city on the border of Arnon and complains of the delay, asking whether he is not able to promote him to honour; Balaam answers that he can speak only the word God puts in his mouth

schools.summary: Calvin makes the scene a study in superstition, which cringes to its prophets while cherishing a pride that breaks out in expostulation, and reads Balaam’s answer as a diplomat’s, signifying that he would have complied so far as civility required and pleading his office as the only obstacle; Gill gives the opening words as a request to say no more of what is past.

Henry reads the meeting as two confederates with unequal expectations, turns the king’s deference into a reproach against the cold reception given to Christ’s ambassadors, hears offended dignity in the complaint and makes promotion an argument for coming to God, and finds Balaam’s answer doubtful rather than noble.

Clarke calls the reply a noble resolution faithfully kept, since Balaam would not displease God even for wealth and honour, and says many who slander him have not half his piety; Wesley places the meeting near the camp of the people to be cursed.

Ellicott corrects the place to the city of Moab and renders the border clause of the Arnon flowing at its extremity; Keil and Delitzsch identify the frontier town as a former capital reduced by Sihon’s conquest, and read Balaam’s reply as an attempt to lower expectations while still concealing from the king what he had concealed from the messengers.

debates: How to read Balaam’s answer to the king. Clarke takes it as a noble resolution to which he was faithful; Henry hears a man hedging and gladly cursing if he could; Calvin allows it breathes piety at first sight and reads it as civility pleading office; Keil and Delitzsch treat it as tactical, lowering expectations while suppressing the same part of the truth he had suppressed before.

39.pericope_label: Balaam goes with Balak to Kirjath-huzoth, where oxen and sheep are offered and sent to Balaam and the princes; and on the morrow Balak brings him up into the high places of Baal to see the utmost part of the people

schools.summary: Gill weighs sacrifice against feast and allows both, since part of an idol offering was commonly eaten, and takes the high place as chosen for worship as well as for the view; Calvin reads the sumptuous reception as a technique of blandishment meant to shame the prophet out of refusing a liberal king, and infers from the choice of a heathen temple that Balaam had no fixed views about the service of God but was one of the trimmers who mingle heaven with earth.

Clarke takes the sacrifice as seeking the favour of Balak’s gods and perhaps of the Lord too, and supposes the whole host had to be in sight lest the curse fail to reach those unseen; Wesley identifies the high place with the worship of Baal Peor and thinks the sight of so great a host was meant to rouse the prophet’s passion.

Ellicott renders the verb as slaughtered, notes it need mean no more than to slay though commonly used of sacrifice, instances ancient kings who were also priests, and gives both readings of how much of the camp was visible; Keil and Delitzsch argue from place and time that the offerings were supplications for success rather than thanks for a safe arrival, and were made to the God of Israel rather than to Moabite idols, and deny that the high place was chosen for its consecration rather than its view.

debates: Why Balak chose the high place. Gill, Wesley and Calvin take the consecration of the site as part of the motive, Calvin making it a temple chosen to conciliate God’s favour; Keil and Delitzsch deny this and say it was simply the first height from which the camp could be seen.

How much of the camp Balaam saw. Ellicott sets one construction of a later verse, on which the whole army was in view, against the commoner reading and the Targum, on which he saw only the rearmost camp; Clarke and Wesley both assume the whole host was meant to be visible.
